title: Attribution Gates Self‐Belief Updating From Social Feedback
content:
Following small-group interactions, participants received experimentally manipulated positive, negative, or neutral feedback about their traits. Negative and expectancy-incongruent feedback was more likely to be judged manipulated. When feedback was perceived as genuine, self-beliefs shifted systematically with feedback valence. When it was perceived as manipulated, valence-dependent updating disappeared, and expectations became the primary influence. These findings suggest that attributional judgments gate the impact of social feedback on self-beliefs.


ABSTRACT

Social feedback can shape self-beliefs, yet its informational value is often uncertain because it depends on others’ motives and accuracy. We tested how people evaluate the credibility of social feedback and how these credibility-related attributional judgments regulate self-belief updating as a function of feedback valence and expectancy congruence. Participants interacted in small groups and subsequently received anonymous feedback on self-relevant traits. Participants were informed that some feedback might have been manipulated. In fact, the experimenter manipulated the feedback to be positive, neutral, or negative relative to initial self-beliefs. Negative feedback and expectancy-incongruent feedback were more likely to be attributed externally (i.e., judged manipulated). Belief updating critically depended on these credibility judgments: when feedback was judged genuine, self-beliefs updated in a graded, valence-consistent manner from negative to neutral to positive feedback; when feedback was judged manipulated, this valence-dependent updating collapsed and updating was driven primarily by expectations. A three-way interaction further showed that belief updating reflected the combined influence of expected feedback valence, received feedback valence, and credibility attributions. These findings support a two-stage account in which credibility assessments gate whether social information is treated as reliable evidence, with implications for how biased credibility judgments may foster maladaptive self-beliefs relevant to psychopathology.
